doc.title: Jon Hendricks interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Crediting King Pleasure, Eddie Jefferson and Annie Ross
summary: Warns against ego and credits those who came before him in vocalese; Edison and Tesla as example.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: That was my son. Well when you look in jazz history there’s a small number comparatively of real innovators. There’s people that build on the innovations. I think that you’re one of those small number of innovators and gosh, you can take a great deal of pride in that.

Well it’s delicate for me because you must be aware of egoism. Egoism — or is it egotism — I don’t know if there’s a “t” in there or not, and I’m an English major I should know. But anyway you must beware of the ego, the overactivity of the ego. Because man nothing is done alone. If it hadn’t been for King Pleasure, for Eddie Jefferson, for Annie Ross’ “Twisted” and “Farmer’s Market” which were done before Lambert, Hendricks & Ross, I would not have had the road sign to point me toward lyricizing orchestral versions of things. You have to watch out. Whereas it’s true that what Leonard Feather dubbed vocalese was the lyricizing of orchestral things — without that lyricizing of individual horn parts, I doubt if I would have been able to do what I did. I had a lot of help in that. Just as everything else. Everybody has help. Edison never acknowledged the help he had from Tesla. In fact there are some people who say he stole the light bulb from Tesla, as there are facts to support that. But you have to be aware of how you assess yourself, because you can go overboard and you can obscure the contributions of those who came before you. You can stand in their light if you’re not careful. I don’t want to do that.
I don’t want to do that. I’m very aware that if it hadn’t been for these people I may never have done what I did.
